en: 12. Chapter on Contemplating the Tathāgata (End of Section Six).
The "Chapter on Contemplating the Tathāgata," comprising eleven chapters in total, is divided into three parts within the section that correctly presents the fundamental doctrine:
the first nine chapters clarify the realm of the bodhisattva; the next single chapter clarifies the practice of the bodhisattva; and this present chapter clarifies the [fruit] of the bodhisattva.
Regarding "fruit" (*phala*): it refers to the fact that through cultivation, one will necessarily attain a great fruit.
As for the name "Tathāgata," it has already been explained as before.
Regarding "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*): it means to observe; the illuminating discernment of wisdom is called contemplation.

Fearing that those who practice the sublime conduct might cling to the notion of a truly existent Tathāgata and fail to understand the correct contemplation of the distinction between the two bodies, I now teach this correct contemplation so that they may seek realization and attain Buddhahood.
Because it explains the intention behind Vimalakīrti’s arrival and elucidates the sublime essence of the Tathāgata in detail, this chapter is titled "The Chapter on Contemplating the Tathāgata.
Sūtra: At that time, the World-Honored One... [up to] ...contemplating the Tathāgata.
The commentary states:
The Buddha-body is twofold: first, the real; second, the provisional.
Based on these two types, there are two sections in this chapter.

At the beginning, when the Tathāgata poses the question, he clarifies the contemplation of the *dharmakāya* Tathāgata—or perhaps including the *svasaṃbhogakāya*—as evidenced by the passage "realizing all-knowledge" (*sarvajñajñāna*), which clarifies the *svasaṃbhogakāya* because both are substantial bodies (*satkāya*).

Later, when Śāriputra poses the question, it is due to his witnessing the immovable Buddha-activities that the contemplation of the *parasaṃbhogakāya* is clarified; this simultaneously reveals that Śākyamuni, who dwells in a defiled land, is a *nirmāṇakāya* Buddha, as both are provisional bodies (*upāyakāya*).
Śāriputra sighed and praised Vimalakīrti, saying:
"You are truly able to abandon that pure Buddha-field and come to delight in this world-system so full of various defilements.
Thus we know that Akṣobhya is the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body), while Śākyamuni is the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body).

The bodies of all Buddhas do not transcend the ultimate and the provisional; this contemplation is possessed by all Tathāgatas, yet it is through the provisional transformation of Śākyamuni that they are reflected upon according to specific circumstances and causes.

The two bodies—the Dharma-body and the Reward-body—are profound in principle yet largely understood; I rely on this to pose my inquiry, clarifying that the contemplation of the Tathāgata is not merely the contemplation of Śākyamuni’s transformation body.
The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "There are two bodies of the Buddha:
first, the Dharma-body; second, the birth-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
Both the true-thusness Dharma-body and the self-enjoyment body are termed the 'Dharma-body,' because they are both perfected through the accumulation of actual meritorious dharmas."
"The Buddha of Enjoyment for Others (*sāmbhogika-buddha*) and the Transformation Buddha (*nirmāṇa-kāya-buddha*) are both termed 'birth-body' (*janma-kāya*), because they do not possess real virtues.
Based on this topical outline, it is divided into two parts.
The first section contains two sub-sections:
The question comes first and the answer follows;
this is the former.
It restates the prior intention for the purpose of contemplating the Tathāgata.
"How do you perceive the Tathāgata?
Do you perceive his provisional marks or his true body?
Vimalakīrti replied, "I perceive him in such a manner."
The commentary says:
The following is the answer.
It consists of three parts:
This consists of three parts: first, a general heading; second, a detailed explanation; and third, a concluding summary.
This is the first part. Regarding the meaning of the principle of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), it is said:
The body of Śākyamuni is a provisional form adapted to the mundane world, possessing visible characteristics;
the essence of the true Buddha is the emptiness of the nature of all dharmas, being formless and signless, and thus entirely invisible.
Now, observing the true Buddha, I say that in my observation there is nothing at all to be seen.
The *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "If one sees me by means of form, or seeks me by means of sound, such a person has entered upon a wrong path and cannot see me."
Therefore, when one contemplates the Tathāgata, nothing at all is perceived.
The meaning according to principle is as follows:

the Dharma-body, which is ultimate truth, is without marks and without form. Although the self-enjoyment body consists of the five aggregates, it is so subtle and exquisite that even Bodhisattvas on the ten stages cannot know it, let alone those in lower positions.

The essence fills the dharma-realm and cannot be grasped through form, mind, or physical characteristics; furthermore, it is entirely without visibility. Therefore, this is answered in summary: one should contemplate in this manner.
The old version states: "As one contemplates the true mark of one's own body, so too does one contemplate the Buddha.
This "true mark" (shixiang) is *tathatā* (true suchness); this differs slightly from the new version, as it only allows for the interpretation of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Sūtra: "For what reason? [It] does not abide in the present.
Commentary: This is the detailed explanation below.
The Meaning of the Principle of Emptiness states:
Regarding the contemplation of the True Body (dharmakāya) below,
there are two [aspects]:
This consists of a brief explanation followed by a detailed explanation;
this is the brief explanation.

Relying on conventional forms for the sake of transformation, having cultivated [the path] from the past limit, proceeding toward the future limit to guide and transform others, and appearing in the present world to dwell among and teach sentient beings—thus may he be seen.
Ultimate truth is formless because its nature is fundamentally empty; since it has no coming, going, appearing, or abiding throughout the three periods of time, how could it be seen?
Therefore, when one contemplates the Tathāgata, there is nothing at all to be seen.
The *Prajñāpāramitā* further states: "That wondrous body of the Tathāgata is the Dharma-body of the Teacher; that body cannot be seen, and that consciousness cannot cognize it."
The *Yingliyi* (Principles of the Correct Meaning) states:
The subsequent commentary has two parts;
the first, extending up to "serene liberation," clarifies the contemplation of the Dharmakāya.
Following the section on "Realization and Assembly" below, the text clarifies the contemplation of the self-enjoyment body (*svasaṃbhogakāya*).
This section consists of two parts:
first, a brief exposition; second, a detailed exposition.
This is a brief explanation.
For what reason does one perceive nothing at all when contemplating the Dharma-body?
Because it does not belong to the three periods of time.
Regarding the inclusion within the three periods of time, it is because [the object] can be seen.
The Sūtra says: "For what reason? Because its nature is not consciousness.
The Commentary states:

Regarding the meaning of the principle of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the following provides an extensive explanation of contemplating the true body (*dharmakāya*). Although there are various different textual passages, their intended meaning is that the true body is free from all manifold characteristics (*nimitta*).

The aggregates (*skandha*) are empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), yet this is not an absolute [negation]; therefore, one observes that the true nature beyond the aggregates is not consciousness (*vijñāna*).
The meaning according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
what follows is an extensive exposition of the Dharmakāya, which should consist of six sections:

First, it is free from the characteristics of the five aggregates; second, it differs from the bodies of the three realms of existence; third, it accords with the supramundane path; fourth, it dispels both phenomena and non-phenomena; fifth, it is identical to the ultimate truth and transcends the mundane; sixth, it is liberation through the severance of fetters.
This is the first passage.

Since the suchness (*tathatā*) of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) is the Buddha’s Dharma-body, one observes that the suchness of the aggregates is not identical to the five aggregates themselves.
Thus, the *Prajñāpāramitā* says: "To see me by means of form, or to seek me through sound, is to follow a false path; such persons cannot see the Tathāgata."
The "wondrous essence" (miao ti) of the added [nature] is precisely the Dharmakāya Buddha; its substance cannot be seen and consciousness cannot know it.

However, when the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and other texts state, "Having abandoned impermanent form, one attains eternal form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so," this refers to the Saṃbhogakāya Buddha; therefore, there is no contradiction.
Regarding the statement in the old sūtra, "not contemplating form, not contemplating the suchness of form, not contemplating the nature of form," according to the principle of emptiness:

"form" refers to that which possesses characteristics; "suchness" refers to the characteristic of emptiness; and "nature" refers to causes and conditions. Since form belongs to causes and conditions, it is entirely devoid of intrinsic nature.
According to the meaning of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*:

"Sound" refers to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*); "suchness" refers to the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*); and "nature" refers to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
These three depend upon linguistic expression; however, in the case of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), expression is set aside, and therefore none of these are observed.
Although this interpretation contradicts the newly translated text, its meaning may be considered the same.
The Sūtra says: "Not abiding in the four elements... up to being far removed from the three impurities.
The Commentary states:
Second, it differs from the three realms of existence (tridhātu) and the body. There are six [points of difference]:
first, it does not abide within the four elements (catvāri mahābhūtāni)—earth, water, fire, and wind—because it is not composed of these four.
Second, it is identical to the realm of empty space, being without any obstruction, for it takes only empty space as its metaphor.
Third, it is not the six internal sense bases, because its nature of arising is eternally constant.
The old translation says, "the six entrances have no accumulation," because they do not take the accumulation of the six objects as their intrinsic nature.
They are the pathways of the six sense organs within the four realms of existence, which are realized through right wisdom.
Fifth, it is unmixed with the three realms because it is purely untainted (*anāsrava*).
Sixth, it is free from the three stains, as its very essence is the removal of the stains of greed, hatred, and delusion.
Sūtra: It accords with the three liberations and reaches the state of being unobstructed by obstacles.
The commentary states:
There are three types of supramundane paths that accord with the truth. They are as follows:
The first [aspect] accords with the three liberations; the essence of the three liberations consists of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).
The Dharma-body is the object of sublime wisdom and accords with the correct wisdom that takes it as its cognitive support.

Second, regarding the "Threefold Clear Knowledge" (tisro vidyāḥ): the three knowledges of recollecting past lives, the divine eye, and the exhaustion of outflows sever ignorance regarding the three time periods and illuminate the three times through and through; therefore, they are called the Threefold Clear Knowledge.
"To arrive" means to reach.
"Reaching the three knowledges" refers to the wisdom of enlightenment (*bodhi-jñāna*) and the Buddha’s Dharma-body, which are the three knowledges that can reach [this state] in accordance with it.

This essence of *tathatā* (suchness) is not called a "knowledge" because it is untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*), but rather because it is the true nature of wisdom; thus, the meaning of "knowledge" is explained.

It is not that which arrives that is called "arrival," but rather its essence is that which is arrived at; the meaning of "attainment" (*prāpti*) is explained by virtue of its nature as that which arrives.

Third, it reaches the limit of all phenomena without obstruction: this nature of *tathatā* reaches all phenomena, or because the category of cognitive obstructions is unobstructed and unimpeded, reaching the ultimate boundary.
Sūtra: “The limit of reality is not a limit, for its nature is free from both. Commentary:
This refutes four things: phenomena, non-phenomena, the limit of reality, and the absence of a limit.
There are forty-seven phrases, of which twenty-nine were previously present and three have been added here.

All these phrases exclusively negate attachment; they are merely conventional designations and merely conceptual constructions. None of them constitute the intrinsic nature of the Dharma-body, because such designations and conceptual constructions do not accord with ultimate reality.
Now, to preclude this [misconception], it is said that they are not.
Furthermore, as in the first case, although it is the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), it is not the limit of names and conceptual discrimination.
The same applies to the two aspects of *tathatā*: they are not a fixed *tathatā*.

Thirdly, because it is eternally non-abiding and is not a cognizing wisdom (*prajñā*), it is not associated [with other factors]. This is because "association" refers to such things as time, basis, location, and object; furthermore, both the object of True Suchness (*tathatā*) and the wisdom are equally free from these.
Sūtra: "Not produced by causes" up to "not different from the beginning.
Commentary: This consists of six phrases.

First, it does not arise from causes and conditions; second, it is neither existent nor non-existent in character; third, it is neither characterized by self nor by other; fourth, it is neither identical nor different; fifth, it is not the characterized object; sixth, it is not the characterizing agent.
The immediate cause is solely the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*); the remote conditions are the remaining three conditions.

That which is characterized is what is manifested, and that which characterizes is what manifests; regarding these two, whether they are identical or distinct, or whether they share the same nature or differ, all such positions are untenable.
The old interpretation states: "Not being of a single characteristic" is emptiness;
"not being of a different characteristic" is existence.
"Not being of its own characteristic" is its own characteristic.
It is not the mark of another, nor the common mark.
It is not the absence of marks, for it dispels marks;
it is not the grasping of marks, for it is the grasping of marks.
Sūtra: “It is neither this shore, nor reaching [the other shore], nor abiding, nor departing.
Commentary: This consists of nine phrases.
The three—going, coming, and their combination—are unified as one.
This shore refers to birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*); the other shore refers to nirvāṇa; and the middle stream refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*).
"Neither both" means it is neither internal nor external.
"Not non-simultaneous" means it is neither not internal nor not external.

The old translation states: "While transforming sentient beings, one contemplates quiescent extinction yet does not undergo eternal extinction. This means that while contemplating sentient beings, one should contemplate quiescent extinction, yet it is not an eternal extinction.
It is not that the Dharmakāya can perform transformations; it is neither this body nor that body.
Because it is neither this nor that, it cannot be manifested as "this" or "that"; it cannot be known by worldly wisdom, nor can it be apprehended by the discriminating mind.
Sūtra: "Without name, without mark, up to there being not even the slightest meaning that can be spoken.
Commentary: This consists of seven phrases.
"Name" refers to that which expresses; "characteristic" refers to that which is expressed.
It does not abide within the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) nor within the body, yet it is not separate from them.
There is no slight essence that can be pointed out, and there is no slight principle that can be explained to others.
Sūtra: From "no giving" and "no stinginess" up to "no wisdom" and "no delusion.
Commentary: These consist of six phrases, as the six perfections and the six hindrances correspond to one another respectively.
Sūtra: "Neither truth nor falsehood, up to: not to be grasped. Commentary:
This consists of eight phrases; "truth" (*satya*) refers to reality, while "falsehood" (*mṛṣā*) refers to unreality.
All linguistic expressions, ritual acts, and conditioned activities universally sever delusions.
The Sūtra says: "From non-characteristics to equality and equality.
The Commentary states:
This consists of six phrases:
it is neither characterized by marks nor devoid of marks; it is neither something produced nor not produced.
Its essence is beyond calculation and transcends all reckoning; its essence is without obstruction.
The preceding and succeeding are similar and equal: as the preceding is, so is the succeeding;
as the preceding is equal, so is the succeeding.
Sūtra: Identical with the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), reaching the state of neither perception nor non-perception.
The commentary states:
"The five [verses] share in the transcendence of the mundane.
The first two lines share in the truth; the following seven lines transcend the mundane."
The *bhūtakoṭi* (the limit of reality) is non-conceptual wisdom; it has no object of perception, and the *dharmakāya* is identical to it.

The *dharmadhātu* (the realm of phenomena) is the nature (*dharmatā*) of all meritorious qualities; the *dharmakāya* is equal to it, because they are identical in essence through their shared meaning.
These two phrases are identical to reality (*tathatā*).
That which can designate is the designator; that which is designated is the designated.
All things that accord with nature possess the nature of both the designator and the designated.
"Measurement" (māna) means deliberation; the same applies to the three meanings [of the other terms].
Sūtra: "Free from all fetters, one is serenely liberated.
Commentary: [As follows:]
Sixth is liberation through dissociation (*visamyoga-vimukti*).
Because it does not consist of discrete entities, it is called the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
The Sūtra states: "It realizes and attains all things, pervading everything."
The commentary states:
Looking downward at the self-enjoyment body, there should be seventeen phrases in total.
The first four phrases clarify the substance of the retribution body.
The subsequent thirteen phrases concern the relinquishing of attachment to phenomena;
this is the first [of them].

By means of the correct wisdom that takes [these] as its object, one is able to realize and comprehend them, thereby accomplishing all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*) and the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñā*).
When mind and object are both in profound stillness, principle and spirit meet; thus, it is called equality.
One attains the non-dual fundamental nature of sentient beings, for this fundamental nature, true suchness, is without differentiation.
Alternatively, this compassion and wisdom equally take sentient beings as their object, for there is no duality between them.
"To attain" (dai) means to reach.

To reach the non-differentiated nature of all phenomena is precisely this mind-intelligence (*cittajñāna*); it is the Buddha’s bodhi and the self-enjoyment body (*svasaṃbhogakāya*), which pervades all things and is omnipresent because it is equal to *tathatā*.
The old translation says "equality of all wisdoms. Having attained the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*), all Buddhas are equal.
Regarding their identity with sentient beings: one contemplates that all sentient beings are non-dual, because their true nature is the same.
Sūtra: From being without fault and without weariness up to being without arising and without exhaustion.
Commentary: The following thirteen phrases are free from all attachments.
This consists of seven points.
"Offense" (*āpatti*) refers to the fruit of suffering, because it is to be reviled and loathed.
"Transgression" (*āgas*) refers to karma and afflictions, because they are extreme faults.
"Turbidity" refers to the three types of karma arising from the inverted views of non-Buddhists;
it is subsumed under the turbidity of lack of faith because the Noble Teaching serves as its antidote.
"Filth" refers to the three types of karma that defile the continuum, giving rise to such obstructive karma based upon them.
Furthermore, the establishment of doctrines regarding purification that are subsumed under the view of nihilism is called "corruption" (dūṣaṇa).
The obstruction to the vision of true selflessness that is subsumed under the view of a personal identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) is called "turbidity" (kaṣāya).
All things are unobstructed and without attachment, free from the three types of discrimination, the seven types of discrimination, the eight types of discrimination, and so forth.

They are neither produced by anything nor born from anything; this negates both spontaneous production and birth, as well as the production and birth of any truly existent phenomena. Furthermore, there is no reality or unreality, nor is there any real arising or ceasing.
Alternatively, there may be no arising from any destination, nor any beginning or end of such arisings.
As the Sūtra says: "There has never been, nor will there ever be, that which can be described. Commentary:
This consists of six points.
Since there is no substantial reality in the past or future, there is neither what has been nor what is yet to come.
Because there are no five fears and no taints or defilements, one is unmoved by the eight winds; thus, there is neither sorrow nor joy.
Having reached the ultimate consummation, there is neither longing nor aversion.
The [periods of] two, three, and seven [days], etc., are not objects of conceptual discrimination; they can only be realized through wisdom.
It is said to be ineffable because no words can realize it; its nature is dependent origination (*paratantra*), yet it is also free from all attachments.
Sūtra: “World-Honored One, Tathāgata, this is called wrong contemplation.
Commentary: This concludes the rectification.

This contemplation of the two kinds of true bodies—the Dharma-body and the Reward-body—is called "right contemplation," because provisional [teachings] are regarded as true and false views are excluded.
Sūtra: At that time, Śāriputra arrived in the Sahā world.
The commentary states:
The second section below contains Śāriputra’s inquiry.

It is based on his vision of Akṣobhya Buddha that he cultivates the contemplation of the *parasaṃbhogakāya*, while simultaneously revealing that Śākyamuni, who dwells in a land of impurity, is a *nirmāṇakāya* Buddha.
Within the section on the provisional body, there are four parts:
first, Śāriputra’s inquiry; second, the Tathāgata’s extensive response; third, the joy in beholding Abhirati; and fourth, Śāriputra’s praise.
This is the first question.
Not only did Śāriputra fail to recognize the origin [of the goddess], but he also used this inquiry to manifest the retribution of others.
Since the goddess spoke of her "original nature," he asked where she had come from, rather than asking where she had departed from.
Since Vimalakīrti had come for the sake of sentient beings, he questioned [the Buddha] regarding the coming but not the going.
The Sūtra states: "The World-Honored One said, 'You should question him.
The Commentary says:
The Tathāgata’s extensive response below consists of three parts:
first, a response by means of inference to reveal the principle; second, a response through personal testimony to illustrate the facts.
The old version says, "Inquiry to Vimalakīrti," yet it lacks the text for the Buddha’s inquiry.
Furthermore, below, the Buddha speaks of himself, and there is no place for an inquiry; thus, it is utterly inconsistent.
This initial section has two parts:
This is the first instance where, after an initial inquiry,
the Buddha questions the other in return. Since Śāriputra asked about the origin of a certain matter, the Buddha answered by recounting his own life story.
Because I have attained realization of the profound principle through this present inquiry, I ask you these questions.
After some time, Śāriputra came to be born in this land.
The commentary says:
There are eight types of questions posed to others:

first, the direct question; second, the counter-interrogation; third, the direct answer; fourth, the reprimanding inquiry; fifth, the direct response; sixth, the citation of a question; seventh, the confirmation; and eighth, the presentation of the correct [view].
This is the first [section].
The Sūtra says: “Vimalakīrti said: ‘...until one can pass away and be reborn?
The Commentary says:
This is a second round of interrogation.
If [the truth] is to be fully known, then cessation is to be realized.
This question is posed while distinguishing between the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*), at the very moment of realizing the principle.
[Sūtra]: Śāriputra said, "...up to the point of passing away and being reborn. [Commentary]:
This is the third direct answer.
Having correctly entered into principle, there is not the slightest extinction or birth.
The Sūtra says: "Vimalakīrti spoke... until he came to be born in this land.
The Commentary says:
The fourfold interrogation has two parts:
first, the interrogation regarding the prior [cause]; second, the further interrogation.
This is the first [section].
Sūtra: Furthermore, Śāriputra... up to... came to be born here. Commentary: This is the first [section]. Sūtra: Furthermore, Śāriputra... up to... came to be born here. Commentary:
This is a further inquiry and reprimand.
Above, one exhausts the matter through principle; in principle, there is no such thing as death or birth.
Below, one interrogates through phenomena; in phenomena, there is no such thing as death or birth.
Sūtra: Śāriputra spoke, [extending] down to "there is death and rebirth. Commentary:
This is the fifth direct answer.
Since transformations are not real, they have neither arising nor perishing.
The Sūtra says: “Vimalakīrti spoke... ‘Are they like illusions and transformations?
The Commentary says:
Sixth, the introductory question:
citing the teaching as a question in order to investigate the fundamental tenets.
Sūtra: Śāriputra said, "So it is, so it is."
The commentary states:
The seven seals are thus validated.
From the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, from the words of Vimalakīrti until "will come to be born in this land."
The commentary states:
The eightfold array is correct.
Previously, since principle (*li*) is equal and already devoid of death and birth, why now, with phenomena (*shi*) being identical, would there be any need to pose a question?
There are two parts:
first, the direct analogy; second, the detailed exposition.
This is the former.
Sūtra: Furthermore, Śāriputra, [it extends] up to the characteristic of the continuity of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Commentary: The following section provides a detailed exposition.
There are two parts:
first, the specific explanation of the characteristics of death and rebirth; second, the formal exposition thereof.
Now, what is called "death" refers to the characteristic of the cessation and extinction of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
"Arising and arising" refers to the characteristic of the continuity of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Its essence is neither eternal nor annihilated; because it resembles those two characteristics, it is called "dying and being born.
The Sūtra says: "Although a Bodhisattva passes away, they do not fall into the state of practicing evil dharmas."
The commentary states:
This is the correct explanation.
Although it is shown that there is passing away, one does not sever virtuous conduct; thus, there is no characteristic of severance.
Although he manifests birth, he does not continue in unwholesome conduct; this is the mark of impermanence.
This passing away and being born is free from the marks of annihilation or permanence.
Sūtra: At that time, the World-Honored One... arrived at being born in this realm.
The commentary states:
The following section provides answers to clarify the matters.
There are three parts:
This consists of three parts: first, the Buddha’s pointing out; second, Śāriputra’s praise; and third, Vimalakīrti’s questions and answers.
This is the first part.
There is a world in the eastern direction named Abhirati (Wonderful Joy), so called because its various adornments give rise to joy upon being seen.
The Buddha's name is Akṣobhya, which in this language means "Immovable.
Because he is not disturbed by the eight winds and is not invaded by the four māras, remaining eternally peaceful and unchanging, he is called Immovable.
For the sake of delivering sentient beings, this arises from that.
Sūtra: Śāriputra spoke, [extending] to "in many places of impurity. Commentary:
This was praised by Śāriputra as being pure because it is a land of retribution for others;
this is called defiled because it is a land of transformation.
Sūtra: Vimalakīrti said, “One should dwell in association with those who possess the characteristics of ultimate bliss.
Commentary: Below follows the dialogue between Vimalakīrti and [the interlocutor].
There are five.
This is from the *Vimalapraśna-sūtra*. Śāriputra said: "...until all darkness is extinguished."
The commentary states:

The two Śāriputras replied that as light arises and darkness ceases, they do not delight in confusion; this implies that Bodhisattvas truly do not delight in dwelling together with those who produce evil.
Sūtra: Vimalakīrti said, "I have come to Jambudvīpa. Commentary:
This is the third inquiry regarding the stainless.
To resolve this doubt, it is asked:
"If they do not delight in the manifold [world], for what reason have Bodhisattvas come to be born here?
Thus, this question is posed.
Sūtra: From the words "Śāriputra said" up to "for the sake of producing illumination. Commentary:
This is the fourth response by Śāriputra.
Sūtra: Vimalakīrti said, "...up to the darkness of afflictions.

The phrasing is clear and the meaning is easy to understand; therefore, it is not explained again. Sūtra: At that time, the great assembly... down to the assembly of śrāvakas. The two Buddhas manifested by command.
Why does the Tathāgata not manifest himself for them to see, but instead commands Vimalakīrti to appear?
This is because he wishes to demonstrate that even a lay devotee who assists in the Buddha’s transformation of beings still displays supernatural powers, let alone the Tathāgata himself.

Furthermore, because one wishes to show that all Bodhisattvas are born in the Pure Land, there must necessarily be a Body of Enjoyment for Others; thus, knowing that the body of Śākyamuni is a provisional transformation for others, there is no logical contradiction in causing that [original land] to manifest.

It describes the realm of the vessel, which is the city of the King; and the realm of sentient beings, consisting of bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, men and women, both great and small.

The commentary states:

there are three [aspects]:

consisting of ten [sections].
All three types of wisdom are capable of providing benefit;
yet merely hearing this teaching is already called a great benefit, for it can ultimately and forever uproot birth and death—how much more so the six virtues:
first, faith and understanding; second, receiving and upholding; third, reading; fourth, reciting; fifth, explaining; and sixth, practicing.

The *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya* states: "That is to say: writing it down, making offerings to it, giving it to others, listening to it, reading it, receiving and upholding it, correctly expounding it, reciting it, as well as reflecting upon it and practicing it."
Regarding the practitioner of the ten dharmas: because they obtain an immeasurable and supreme mass of merit that is inexhaustible, they ceaselessly engage in the gathering of others.

first, obtaining precious wealth with one's hands;
if obtained by hand, one then acquires the treasure of the Dharma, which can bring great benefit because it is worthy of being cherished.

Second, through resolute belief and understanding, one perpetuates the lineage of the Buddhas;
if one possesses such faith and understanding, one then continues the Buddha-body, which is the body of uninterrupted succession.
Faith-understanding is itself faith; together with the wisdoms of hearing and reflection, it serves as the cause for Buddhahood, and is therefore called "succession.
Sūtra: "If all sentient beings reach the unsurpassed dharma of cessation..."
The commentary states:
This consists of two phrases.
First, recitation serves as the superior companion.
Whether reading or reciting, one’s body is the Bodhisattva and the teaching is the Dharma-Buddha; when reading and reciting are never abandoned, these two are called the supreme companions.
By upholding these two, one thereby encompasses the True Dharma.
If one upholds [this teaching], one thereby embraces the True Dharma.
"Embracing" means to encompass and integrate; "upholding" means to receive and internalize.
To maintain it within the mind, never forgetting it, constitutes the embracing and receiving of the unsurpassed True Dharma.
The unsurpassed true Dharma is, in essence, the Mahāyāna’s teaching, principle, practice, and fruit.
[From the] Sūtra: “If there is one who makes offerings... up to the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna). Commentary:
This consists of two statements.

those who study this Dharma should regard the Buddha’s body as their own; since the causes for the *nirmāṇakāya* and *sambhogakāya* already exist within their own bodies, that which they study is the Dharmakāya Tathāgata, and thus they are able to make offerings.
Those who study this Dharma should know that the Tathāgata is present within their very home.
Second, transcribing it gathers merit and wisdom.
If one transcribes and makes offerings to this Dharma, one thereby gathers and sustains both merit and wisdom, for this sutra is capable of generating these two: merit and wisdom.
Sūtra: "If there are those who rejoice [in this merit], they will reach the stage of non-retrogression.
Commentary: This consists of two phrases.
First, rejoicing constitutes the gift of Dharma.

When one rejoices, it becomes a gift of Dharma; for this Dharma can bring benefit to sentient beings, therefore, if one rejoices so that it may circulate and does not create obstacles to others' cultivation and study, that person who rejoices thereby accomplishes the gift of Dharma.
Second, preaching that which is near to non-retrogression:
by explaining a single four-line verse to others, one becomes close to non-retrogression.
Regarding "a single four-line verse": four lines constitute one verse.
The place where these four lines of this principle are fully complete is called a "four-line verse" (catuspāda-gāthā).
There are four types of non-retrogression:
first, faith; second, stage; third, realization; and fourth, practice, as previously explained.
According to what is appropriate, one draws near to this non-retrogression. Sūtra:

"‘Sugata’ (Well-Gone) means that throughout the long night, he has been endowed with all aspects of the two benefits [for self and others].

Now that the Buddha has reached the fruit and has already successfully departed, he is called "Well-Gone" (*sugata*).
As for "Knower of the World," it means that he has thoroughly and skillfully penetrated all aspects of both the world of sentient beings and the physical world of the vessel.

Regarding the receptacle world, it refers to the worlds of the ten directions, such as the east, because he thoroughly understands their infinite formation and destruction.

The Unsurpassed Great Man, the Tamer of Men, is so called because his wisdom is peerless and unsurpassed.

There are further distinct instances, as found in the *Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of the Thousand Buddhas* and the *Sūtra of Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata*, as well as in the *Commentary on Maitreya’s Ascent to Heaven*, which explains that the first, Krakucchanda Buddha; the second, Kanakamuni Buddha; the third, Kāśyapa Buddha; and the fourth, Śākyamuni Buddha, have already appeared in the world.

Regarding the subsequent future appearances in the world, the sequence of kalpas, and their respective temporal positions, each is explained exactly as in the *Commentary on the Birth Above* (*Shangsheng shu*).
The sutra states: "At that time, Dharmapāla shall arrive; he is none other than my own person."
The commentary states:
This is none other than Candracchattra.
Because he upheld and protected this Dharma to manifest his filial devotion to his parents, he performed the offering of the Dharma and has now attained Bodhi.
Exhort all sentient beings that they too should, like me, protect, uphold, study, practice, and perform offerings of the Dharma.
Sūtra: "O Lord of Devas, you should know... [this] is the most supreme."
The commentary says:
The following section consists of two parts: first, praising the Dharma; second, exhorting [the practitioner] to cultivate it for its supreme benefits.
The first part is a praise, and the latter part is an exhortation; this is the praise.
"Most Honored One" is because his practice has reached the highest pinnacle.
It is the most excellent practice because it transcends all;
it is the most supreme because its practice is foremost;
it is the most wondrous because its practice is subtle goodness.
"Unsurpassed" means that there is nothing prior to it.
Alternatively, following the sequence, the first four are most excellent because they provide offerings of food and drink, clothing, bedding, and medicinal requisites.
This single type is unsurpassed because it is superior to the preceding four; thus, its essence is unsurpassed.

Furthermore, through the offering of the Dharma, one can attain the Dharma-body consisting of the five untainted aggregates (*anāsrava-skandha*), namely: morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; these are to be assigned respectively.

Alternatively, one may attain the pure dharmadhātu and the four wisdoms—the great perfect mirror wisdom, the wisdom of equality, the wisdom of wondrous observation, and the wisdom of accomplished action.
These are assigned respectively, and thus they are called the five supremacies.
Sūtra: "For this reason, O Lord of Devas, [one should practice] up to not using material wealth. Commentary:
This is an exhortation.

The fundamental intention of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is to cause sentient beings to practice the Dharma so that they may attain transcendence; therefore, the offering of the Dharma is superior to the offering of material wealth.

Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, in the "Assembly of King Śūra," states: "Two types of persons are far removed from kings, thieves, and others such that they cannot invade the great treasury; yet for hundreds of thousands of great kalpas, they hear the Dharma with joy, yet upon hearing it, they neither uphold nor bestow it."

Protecting the true Dharma with the great bodhicitta, practicing and making offerings according to the teachings, and maintaining a mind of equality that benefits both self and others—this is what is called truly making offerings to the Buddha.
"Among all forms of offering, the offering of the Dharma is supreme.
Even secular texts say: 'Though one may daily slaughter the three kinds of livestock for sustenance, if this contravenes the will of one's parents, it is still considered unfilial.'"
"How much more so for those who have transcended the world?
For the Buddha originally did not hope for material offerings.
As the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "To daily sacrifice bodies as numerous as three Ganges Rivers is inferior to upholding even four lines of verse."
Therefore, the supreme wealth of the Dharma-offering is immeasurable.
Its growth and fruition are as vast as the elements becoming atoms;
it can extinguish evil just as the sun dispels darkness, and thus no worldly analogy can suffice.

14. Chapter on the Entrustment (End of Part Six). Following the two chapters on the praise and transmission of the gift of Dharma—which constitute the praise and transmission of the teaching—this present chapter concerns the entrustment and transmission of the teaching.

If one does not bestow [the teaching] with meticulous care, there is a fear that the Dharma may be treated with contempt or remain obscure; therefore, it is entrusted with gravity so that faith may arise and study may proceed.
To bestow through words is called "entrustment" (*shuku*); to inform repeatedly is termed "accumulation" (*rui*).

This chapter explains this extensively and is titled "The Chapter on Entrustment. Sūtra: At that time, the Buddha addressed [the assembly] until the words, "I entrust them to you. Commentary: At that time, the Buddha addressed the assembly, saying: "Śāriputra, listen attentively. What I have taught and manifested throughout my entire life—these Dharma gates, these profound and subtle teachings, and these various practices for attaining Buddhahood—I now all entrust to you. You must uphold, recite, and explain them for the sake of future sentient beings, so that they may all attain the path of the Tathāgata. Commentary: This section clarifies the meaning of "entrustment" (parindanā). It is called "entrustment" because the Tathāgata, having completed his work of teaching and transforming sentient beings, now transfers the responsibility for upholding and propagating the Dharma to others. This is like a king who, having entrusted the governance of his realm to a capable minister, retires from active administration. Furthermore, it is called "entrustment" because the Tathāgata, fearing that after his parinirvāṇa the true Dharma might decline, has now transferred the task of protecting and maintaining the Dharma to Mahākāśyapa and others. It is also called "entrustment" because the Tathāgata, wishing to ensure that the Dharma will not perish after his passing, has now committed the responsibility of its preservation to the Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas. Moreover, it is called "entrustment" because the Tathāgata, desiring that the Dharma be widely propagated in the future, has now charged the Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas with the duty of its dissemination. Finally, it is called "entrustment" because the Tathāgata, wishing to cause the Dharma to endure for a long time, has now assigned the task of its long-term maintenance to the Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas. The first section further has three parts:

This fruit, gathered from the ocean of the Noble Conduct, is entrusted to you because its essence and function are vast.
This sutra is protected by the arrival of such scriptures.

This clarifies the supreme excellence of the Dharma.
Abiding by the power of the Buddha’s majesty, it does not perish because of this.
Because the Buddha’s majestic power protects them, they are free from calamities and misfortunes.
Sūtra: You shall reach the Tathāgata and never again fall into concealment or extinction.
Commentary: It says:
This is intended to ensure its transmission and continuity in the final age; "receiving" (*parigraha*) refers to providing protection.
"Upholding," "receiving," and "protection" are synonymous terms.
Sūtra: Why is this so? ... up to: immeasurable benefits.
The commentary states:
The preceding section issues the command for practice; the following section explains the reason why.
This consists of two parts:
First, the benefits and harms of two types of people are clarified; second, the person and the Dharma are entrusted.
Within the first part, there are again two sections:
first, the clarification of harm; second, the clarification of benefit.
This is the first [category].
Herein there are two types of persons: first, those who, though not yet having generated the great resolve (*mahācitta*), have already planted superior roots of goodness;
second, those who, having already generated the great resolve, possess vast resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), which refers to the stage prior to the [ten] stages (*bhūmi*).
Among the thirteen stages (*vihāra*), all minds prior to the [first] stage are termed "conduct through resolute belief" (*adhimukti-caryā*); therefore, resolute belief is predominant.

If ordinary beings prior to the stage do not hear the sūtras, those who have not yet resolved their minds cannot resolve them, and those who have already resolved them cannot progress; this is termed "retrogression from the field of resolute belief."
Sūtra: If they are able to hear it, they will receive it with joy up to the crown of their heads. Commentary:
This clarifies the benefit of hearing the Dharma.
The old [commentary] states that "generating the bodhicitta" constitutes the first [stage] and "delighting in the Great Dharma" the second;
thus, it sequentially assigns them to faith-delight and receiving upon the crown.
However, since "should generate" and "should delight" carry the same meaning as the new text, there is no fault in this either.
Sūtra: "I shall now cause that which is most extensive to be widely proclaimed and disseminated.
Commentary: This constitutes the entrustment of both the person and the Dharma.

Entrusting this to others so that they may protect and mind it without obstruction, and though they have heard this sutra, entrusting the Dharma to them so that they may practice it and widely proclaim and disseminate it.
Sutra: "Maitreya, you should know... up to the Seal of the Bodhisattva’s Characteristics."
The commentary states:
The following sets forth virtues and faults;
there are three [sections]:
First the heading, next the manifestation, and finally the explanation.
This is the first [part].
There are two kinds of seals (mudrā):
First is the seal of signlessness (*animitta-mudrā*), which has already been explained above.
Second is the seal of signs (*sanimitta-mudrā*), which is this one.
"Sign" (*nimitta*) refers to a form or characteristic; "seal" (*mudrā*) refers to certainty.
The determination of characteristics is called the "seal of characteristics" (*lakṣaṇamudrā*).
These two teachings are called "seals" because they seal a single bodhisattva.
Sūtra: "What are the two [teachings] up to the entry into the seal of characteristics?"
The commentary states:
This manifestation has two aspects:
The first part provides the inquiry, and the latter part reveals the answer; this is the former.
First, one accepts the flowery words, and the principle follows accordingly whether they are crooked or straight.
Second, regarding the profound Dharma, the very nature and characteristics that one delights in and so forth constitute the essence of the seal of characteristics (*lakṣaṇamudrā*).
"Entering" means realizing through understanding.
Sūtra: "If there are bodhisattvas... up to bodhisattvas who have long practiced."
The commentary states:
This explanation has two parts.
The first passage is understandable; it is because one receives the text but does not receive the meaning.
Regarding the second, that the Bodhisattva is without defilement, without attachment, and so forth, is itself the profound Dharma.

Regarding this fearlessness, having heard it, one believes and understands it, and even practices it; through this, one attains supramundane pure faith, and is thus called "one who has long practiced.
For if one does not study for a long time, one will ultimately be unable to believe in and delight in this.
Sūtra: "O Hui, you should know that [this leads] to the most profound dharma-patience.
Commentary: The following sets forth the characteristics of error.
There are two [sections], which sequentially clarify the first two types of bodhisattvas.
The first [section] further has three parts:
first, the heading; second, the exposition; and third, the conclusion.
This is the first [point].
Regarding the "patience of the dharma" (*dharmakṣānti*): it is the wisdom-patience obtained regarding the teachings on the truths in the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*), due to four conditions.
A beginner bodhisattva does not attain the first stage.
Sūtra: "What are the four? From what do they arise?
Commentary: The following clarifies this.
There are two parts:
first, the inquiry; second, the exposition.
Within the exposition, there are two further divisions:
The first two [types of faith] concern the Dharma, while the latter two concern persons.
This refers to the former.
Regarding that which has not yet been heard, one can give rise to two matters:
First, being startled and fearful, they do not rejoice in their hearts, and thus give rise to opposition.
Second, even if they have heard it, they slander it behind one's back and disparage it in one's presence, saying, "This is not what I have heard before; from where did it come?"
Without any basis, they give rise to slander.
Sūtra: Third, seeing [existence], they proceed to revile it. Commentary:
Regarding these two types of people:
first, those who see and believe in this person but take no pleasure in associating with them, taking no pleasure in honoring them, and taking no pleasure in prostrating before them;
second, those who initially believe in this person but later treat them with physical contempt, increase their mental envy, speak ill of them in their presence, and slander them behind their back.
The old translation combines these four into two gates because the factors and persons are identical.
The sūtra states: "By means of these four conditions, one attains the profound patience regarding dharmas (*gambhīradharmanidhyānakṣānti*). Commentary:
This is the summary verse.
The Sūtra says: "Maitreya, you should know," up to "the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena.
The commentary states:
The subsequent text also consists of three parts; this is the first, the heading.
Regarding "those who attain the continuous realization of the patience toward the non-arising of dharmas," this occurs in the eighth stage (*bhūmi*).

Previously it was stated that those newly training do not attain the first stage; here it is stated that those still in training (*śaikṣa*) do not attain the eighth stage, or perhaps they do not even attain the first stage.
Sūtra: What are the four? They are receiving the instructions and admonitions of the Teacher.
Commentary: This is explained below.
There are two parts:
first, the inquiry; second, the exposition.
The first two concern the person, while the latter two concern the dharma.
First, they slight those who are newly trained;

second, they do not delight in accepting new trainees as their own children, nor do they delight in instructing them by pointing out the points of training, nor do they delight in teaching them wholesome dharmas, nor do they delight in admonishing them to refrain from committing evil.
Due to these two conditions, those who are new to the study find no way to progress.

The commentary states:

There are four kinds of vastness:

first, the vastness of the various immeasurable trainings; second, the vastness of immeasurable merit; third, the vastness of the altruistic intention; and fourth, the vastness of establishing enlightenment—all as explained therein.
That which is "profound" is so because it is difficult to fathom;
that which is "vast" is so because its essence and function are expansive and extensive.
To lack deep reverence for this Dharma, or to hold a mixture of respect and contempt for it, is a fault.
Second, they delight in the gift of material wealth but do not delight in the gift of the Dharma, because they perceive immediate benefit and happiness rather than future benefit.

This concludes [the section].

[As stated above].

should there be one who seeks the true Dharma-vessel of the Mahāyāna, I shall cause them to receive such a sūtra as this with their own hands, and I shall grant them the power of mindfulness so that they may uphold this sūtra and even extensively expound it to others.
Therefore, that we have now attained this faith, understanding, and extensive exposition is entirely due to Maitreya’s power of mindfulness.
Sūtra: From the time of the World-Honored One until the future period of his sustaining protection.
The commentary says:
This concludes the preceding discussion on "receiving" and "exerting power."

This is the third instance in which the World-Honored One offers praise.
Not turning one's three karmas away from it is called "rejoicing.
To embrace and receive [the teaching], provisionally protecting and maintaining it, is most excellent and wondrous.

The commentary says:

This refers to the former.
While the Buddha was present, his majestic spiritual power (*vibhūti*) could naturally provide protection; therefore, after his parinirvāṇa, I shall uphold and protect it.
This region shall be spontaneously protected and maintained, and other realms shall also come to provide defense.
As the Sūtra says: "If a son of good family... [omitted] ...until there is no obstruction.

This person protects [the Dharma] in two ways:
first, by bestowing the power of mindfulness so that they may remember the teachings without forgetting;

At that time, among this assembly, those who had reached this Dharma-gate praised it, saying:

The commentary states:
This clarifies the near and the far.
A *yojana* is what was formerly called a "youxun" (yōushùn).
According to the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, five hundred bows (*dhanus*) constitute one *krośa*, which is two *li*.
Eight *krośas* constitute one *yojana*, which is sixteen *li*.
There is an ancient tradition that some take forty *li* to be one *yojana*; this too is not erroneous.

Within a range of one hundred *yojanas*, they shall be kept in peace and security; neither celestial Māras, non-Buddhists, nor calamities, obstacles, and misfortunes can cause them hindrance, nor will any evil persons find an opportunity to harm them, except where their karma is fixed.

The commentary states:
The aforementioned entrustment is directed toward the Bodhisattvas, encompassing both the Dharma-realm and sentient beings.

To receive [the precepts] by being addressed with a single name is precisely what constitutes upholding the Dharma.
"Inconceivable" means that it transcends the limits of emotional expression.
"Masterful" (*vaśitā*) means spontaneous and effortless.

"Divine transformations" (*ṛddhi-vikurvaṇa*) refer to the wondrous functions of the fruits of supernormal powers; they involve transformations without fixed direction, appearing suddenly where there was nothing.

Praise says:
The third section of this chapter concludes the exposition of the benefits and expresses joy in its dissemination.
Since the Path arises from non-regret and the departure from sorrow and suffering, there is joy.

Because the mind becomes pure through compliance, because it is held in the heart through reflection, and because it is transmitted and practiced through reliance, it is said that one "faithfully accepts and reverently puts it into practice."

In the sixth fascicle of the *Commentary on the Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra*, the author states: On the twenty-seventh day of the twelfth month of the third year of the Xianheng era, having never before perused the commentaries and treatises of the ancient masters, I was nonetheless compelled by the virtuous monks of Pingdeng Temple in Dayuan County, Bingzhou, to lecture upon this old scripture. Thus, while engaged in the course of the lecture, I composed this work to extol its profound purport.
I would study at night and lecture in the morning; as time passed, I grew negligent and never revisited what I had already covered.
Furthermore, in the seventh month of the fifth year, I traveled to the region of Youming Su, where I lectured again on the old scriptures and was finally able to review them once more.

Although the phrasing is sparse, the meaning is dense; although the terminology is shallow, the principle is profound. However, because time was urgently pressing, I was unable to provide a full and detailed account.
I shall now briefly set forth the points where the texts of this scripture differ, and I hope that all virtuous ones will deign to examine them with careful attention.

In the intercalary fifth month of the second year of the Bōan era, after Yangxin of Xingfu Temple finished reading it, the Master Shuo traveled to the capital and learned that the copy held by Qingqing of Zhiyuan Monastery was either complete or partially deficient; this is the version that I have transcribed.

I have further collated this against the original text, correcting errors of transcription wherever I could discern them; as for those points remaining doubtful, I have left them blank, hoping that those who obtain a superior copy will rectify them. May it be well.
By the winged feather of the mountain: Shin.
Regarding this book, although I previously transcribed it using another person’s hand, I have never yet had the opportunity to read it.
Since the third month of this year, my accumulated studies have had some leisure time; for this reason, I respectfully present this for your perusal.
Any errors such as "wu" for "an" or "lu" for "yu" are due to the circularity of successive transcription and copying.
On the first day of the fourth month of the seventh year of Tenpō, the year of Bingshen, I have finished transcribing this at the command of Master Zizhen.
The Śramaṇa from Lake City, Jue.
